item.title: Entering Atomic Design from the screen
item.description: You don’t always have to build from atoms. Sometimes, you need to discover them.Atomic Design is one of the core mental models of modern design systems. It gives us a common language for describing the interface as a hierarchy: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.Brad Frost said from the very beginning that atomic design is not a linear process, but a mental model that allows us to keep both the whole and its parts in view at the same time. The five levels are not steps one through five.From Template to Atoms.However, in practice, most teams apply the model in one direction. This is especially true when they aim to build a component library: they define the smallest reusable parts and assemble larger blocks from them. And the begin to use them all in screens.This habit is so common that many people mistake it for the methodology itself.Product work usually starts from the other side — from the user experience. When we look at a screen, the first question isn’t “what components are used here,” but “what does the user need to do here?” How will they search, filter, compare, select, edit, and so on?This is another entry point into the Atomic Design model. We could say that this is a “scope-first” approach.A component-first approach can obscure the actual structureA “component-first” approach usually begins with an inventory:This is a buttonThis is an inputThis is a badgeThis is a tableThere are two well-known methods that handle this very well: Brad Frost’s Interface Inventory and Nathan Curtis’s Component Cut-Up Workshop. Both are excellent for their intended purpose: describing an existing interface and kicking off the work on the component library.Interface InventoryThe Component Cut-Up WorkshopBut they answer a specific question: “what’s on the screen?” We need to think about the rest ourselves: ”why something is there and what it’s connected to”.Let’s take a typical admin screen with a data table as an example.The user inventory here looks pretty good:Page titlePrimary actionsTab navigationSearch inputFilter inputsSort buttonsPaginationTooltipsetc.What remains behind the scenes is how all of this is interconnected:The status badge is associated with a single row.Sorting rearranges all rows in the dataset. Even though the control itself is located within a single column header.Search and filters change which records are displayed on the screen at all.A primary action like Add people affects the entire page.Tabs can completely replace the content area’s contents.The proximity of elements to one another is a poor guide in all of this. The sort button is the most obvious example: it resides in a column header but affects the entire table. Elements are linked not by their location, but by the scope of their behavior.Thinking in scopesWhen breaking down a screen, we can start with the scope of each action — the set of data or part of the interface that changes when the user triggers that action.For the admin screen above:This isn’t a complete breakdown, but it already highlights a couple of important points.First: each row in the left column answers the same question — what is changing?You might be tempted to add categories like “navigation” or “table header,” but these describe what the control is or where it’s located. That’s a different axis, and mixing the two axes is exactly what will cause the exercise to quietly turn back into an inventory breakdown.Second: tooltips and badges have no scope at all. They don’t change anything. They’re included in the table to indicate that something isn’t a control — just to complete the picture.This breakdown isn’t universal. On a different screen or in a different product, the scopes will be different.It’s not the list that’s carried over, but the process:Start with what the user can do and what they can interact with.Determine what each specific user action will affect.Decide which level should own the logic.This way, we get a structural model of the screen even before we start creating components.Where the logic livesWhen we design components, we think about the library: its versatility, independence, and applicability in contexts we cannot predict.When we design a product, we think about business logic — the parts must come together to form a cohesive user experience.Search, filters, and pagination illustrate this tension quite clearly. As library components, they can appear in different combinations on different screens, so it makes sense to keep them independent.But on this admin screen, they manage a shared dataset:Changing a filter can reset pagination to the first page.A search query with no matches empties the table, and pagination becomes unnecessary.It is impossible to list all such scenarios when documenting individual components, and the components themselves should not be aware of them. The moment the filter component becomes aware of the pagination component, it loses its reusability and begins to carry the business logic of a single specific use case.But something has to manage these connections. In my experience, it’s most convenient to do this at the template level.A slightly different view on the role of a templateIn Atomic Design, templates are page-level objects that position components within a layout and define the content structure: they are about structure, not state.To put it very simply, a template acts as a “dumb” (presentational) component that only knows how it looks and what data it receives from outside.“Smart components” (container components) are capable of managing data, state, and behavior. They are often built as wrappers around “dumb” (presentational) components.This is roughly what I suggest doing with templates. The individual components remain “presentational”: a table knows how to render rows, a filter knows how to return a value, pagination knows how to display a page number — and they’re all independent and unaware of each other. The template is the wrapper that unites them and holds the logic for how they work together.For data-dense product screens, the template level is the natural place not only for layout, but also for:Which zones are on the screen and where they are located.How the zones are connected.The shared state that flows between them.Rules that belong to the screen’s context, rather than to any specific component.I have often seen developers on product teams create wrappers around several library components when they need to reuse the same set of features, such as filters, search, tables, and pagination, that behave as a single unit.Of course, this kind of logic can be documented as a story in Storybook, but developers often prefer to keep it as ready-made modules rather than rebuilding it from scratch every time.Sometimes these wrappers appear spontaneously and end up somewhere in the /components directory alongside buttons and other “presentational” components. However, it’s still better to keep such templates separate.I should clarify: I’m not saying that every template must contain logic or that any logic should be dragged into a template. The criteria are the same as the question about scope:If a rule describes a relationship between areas and is repeated from screen to screen (“changing the filter resets pagination to the first page”), it belongs in a template.If a rule applies to a specific screen and specific data (“disabled users cannot change their role”), that’s at the page level, and the template shouldn’t be touched.A template that knows too much stops being reusable.I believe this is more of an extension than a contradiction to the logic of Atomic Design templates. This is also the clearest distinction between this approach and Component Cut-Up:Cut-up helps the team identify recurring visual elements and turn them into a list of potential components.A scope-first analysis helps understand “what a user can do on the screen, what their actions affect, and which level should be responsible for it”.Same template, different realityA good template is a reusable structure that works across different product contexts. For example, the same template can be used to manage Members, Projects, Invoices, and other pages.The zones remain the same:Page headerPrimary action areaNavigationToolbarContent areaWhat changes are the elements within them: same structure, different content and behavior.This is the moment when a design system becomes more than just a set of components and begins to describe product patterns. This is exactly what most product teams need.Checking the breakdown with real contentAt the page level, we populate the templates with actual content. At this stage, we need to stress test the system and our layout to make sure the structure can handle content it might not have been designed for. Not just for the “happy path,” but also when:When there is no data. For example, when a search query returns no results.While data is loading.When the page opens on a small screen.The text is much longer than intended for the layout.These are just a few scenarios for a particular single screen. Some of them are typical, such as the empty state. Others may be specific. It’s similar to what QA does with edge cases: finding where things break.The difference lies in what “breaking” means. It’s not always a design problem. Often, it’s a sign that the breakdown is incomplete: a certain state or part of it has no owner, or a rule hasn’t been defined for the zone in case it’s empty.When this approach is useful?First, when you need to create a design system for an existing product. When the product already exists, the question isn’t “How do we create components from scratch?” but rather “How do we understand and systematize what already exists?”Second, when there are debates about the boundaries of components. A scope-first breakdown provides both sides with a more neutral way to discuss ownership. Instead of arguing about whether something “looks like” a component, the team can discuss what it affects and which level should own that behavior.Third, when a product has many similar screens. Admin panels, dashboards, CRM tools, settings pages, marketplaces, financial tools, and internal platforms often repeat the same patterns with different data. Scope-first approach helps clarify which parts are truly reusable and which are simply visually similar.And finally — documentation. Product patterns are much easier to describe in terms of their scopes — page actions, object actions, states. Not through a flat list of components. And this is closer to how a user perceives the screen.When this approach doesn’t help?This approach isn’t one-size-fits-all, and based on my experience, I can point out at least two ways to mess it up.The first is to adjust the logic and components to fit a single screen. The temptation is understandable: if the scope model just fits perfectly, you may want to build a library around it. But a screen is a specific use case, while components should live longer. A scope indicates the level at which the logic should reside. It says nothing about how versatile the component itself will be. I’ve encountered this situation very often when product teams were working under pressure, and designers and developers tried to save every new pattern as a component or a design system template.The second is breaking down what’s already clear. On a landing page, settings form, or login screen, the scope map takes up a single line, yet it can still take a long time to analyze. The entire approach rests on two things: screen density and the overall flow between zones. If neither is present, a traditional inventory cut-up will be faster and deliver the exact same result.ConclusionAtomic Design is a versatile model that makes it quite easy to build component libraries. However, teams often try to use it to build interfaces from small parts, taking the “atomicity” of the approach too literally.Day-to-day product work often starts from the other end: a complex screen already exists, and it needs to be understood. This article shows that Atomic Design helps with this as well. Moreover, the result is not just a more precise breakdown into components, but also a clearer understanding of the product pattern behind the screen.For product teams, this is usually what matters most.Thanks for reading! Write in the comments what you think about the topic.Let’s stay in touch! item.title: Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped
item.description: Concorde, nuclear power and Minitel took three different paths. What can they tell us about Europe’s next technological bets?Concorde, nuclear power and Minitel. AI-generated IllustrationI’ve spent the last week walking the streets of Marseille, indulging in my long-desired vacation. My routine was simple and mostly included booking tables at local spots, open for unapologetically short hours. A sense of urgency is a funny concept when applied anywhere in southern Europe. Born & raised in a southern European city, I can really say that.At the Airbnb where I am staying, the skyline is surprisingly busy. The dense, almost panoptical view makes me think about an interesting thing. I wonder whether the atmosphere that I would describe as “clinically relaxed” was different in the past.France in the 1970s was just peak. Unlike today, it was leaping ahead on a bunch of different tracks where bold vision, execution speed and big capital mattered. It was a tight race, and the French were taking the corners perfectly, often taking the lead over the Soviets and Americans.https://medium.com/media/314577821abd2d41fb53a0dda13aa52f/hrefThe thirty years after WW2 are widely known as Trente Glorieuses or “Three Glorious Decades”. Of course, this era was not as perfect as French history documentaries may portray it. France went through a fair share of political crises when re-establishing itself politically, as well as a couple of ugly (post-)colonial wars. Yet eventually, long-lasting peace and transatlantic partnerships finally gave the continent the time and security needed for generational moonshots.Unlike Germany, which was torn in two and heavily destroyed, France enjoyed a more pleasant type of integration and the luxury of deciding its own destiny. That included nationalising critical industries, obtaining nuclear arms and racing towards the edge of technological success.By the late 1970s and early 1980s, French advancements were just bold. One of the quickest nuclear build-ups in history laid the foundations of French energy independence that endure to this day. Minitel — a French version of the internet, before the World Wide Web took over. And of course, a symbol of the supersonic dream: Concorde. Three bold bets on the future. One became a luxury, one became infrastructure, and one became obsolete.Concorde: ahead of timeIf there were ever a thing that I’d be willing to blow an unreasonable amount of money on immediately — it would be a Concorde flight. As a kid with parents in aviation, I am not easily surprised by anything flying, yet Concorde is something different.Six Concordes parked on the apron. Photo courtesy of British Airways; supplied for editorial use.Technically, it wasn’t all French: the two manufacturing facilities were located in Britain and France. That required a lot of coordination and joint effort, yet the French were never shy about taking credit for it.The plane itself was incredibly sophisticated. There was a mechanism for changing the position of the nose section on every take-off and landing to give the pilots a clear view of the runway. Flying at supersonic speeds made the outer surface so hot that the whole plane would actually extend by tens of centimetres during the flight. Also, fuel would be pumped from one tank to another mid-flight to balance Concorde’s centre of gravity.Concorde’s first test flight, Toulouse-Blagnac, 2 March 1969. Photo: André Cros / Archives municipales de Toulouse, 53Fi1931, CC BY-SA 4.0.Concorde could let you beat the clock. With a flight time of around three and a half hours and New York five hours behind London, you could leave at noon and arrive at 10:30 am local time. The whole idea of stitching together the two sides of the Atlantic with a fast-track channel in the air was futurism in reality, a testament to post-war prosperity and a true European “Ad Astra” moment.The cabin was narrow, with just four seats across. Yet it was still a more prestigious flight, with Champagne, caviar and a certificate for breaking the sound barrier. Passengers would sit next to the tiny windows and enjoy watching the plane reach a supersonic speed of Mach 2 live on the built-in indicators. In the 1990s, designer Andrée Putman redesigned Air France’s cabin, using light and restrained details to make the small space feel elegant.Champagne service aboard a British Airways Concorde. Source: Heritage Concorde.Celebrities loved Concorde. No private jet could match the vibe of a cutting-edge aviation unit, leaping forth ahead of its time. Among its passengers were Mick Jagger, Paul McCartney, Catherine Deneuve and, of course, members of the British royal family.Fred Finn beside a Rolls-Royce, with a British Airways Concorde behind him. Source: Gentleman’s Journal.The final flight of Concorde took place on November 26, 2003, when it flew to Filton for preservation. Commercial services had ended the previous month. Its demise had no single cause. Instead, it was a mix of circumstances, including the famous jet crash of 2000, a shrinking market and rising maintenance costs. The oil crisis of 1973 had already made the economics of supersonic travel harder, long before the final retirement. Add to this a limited number of routes (sonic booms restricted supersonic flying over land) and you get the reason why Concorde became a piece of the future that was no longer economically viable.Nuclear: an atomic ramp-upBack in Marseille, I’m pulling out my phone, which I’ve set to a radical “do not disturb” mode, to check the map, as we’re heading to the beach. One of the push notifications that somehow invades my attention span is about upcoming spikes in energy costs. I put my sunglasses away to figure out the route and instinctively dive into noisy news blurbs, wondering if my electricity bill is gonna hurt after I’m back home in Berlin.My electricity bill might be lower if I decided to settle in France. Energy price shocks are hardly new to the French. Back in the seventies, France already had a nuclear industry when oil prices skyrocketed. The crisis then pushed the country to accelerate its reactor build-out.The idea of strategic autonomy and the notion of self-sustaining politics were cornerstones of post-war France. This was the reason why such assertiveness in both the military and civilian parts of the economy was taken to a higher level. Ironically enough, the heart of the nuclear programme ran on American hardware. France had already built reactors of its own design, but chose a different technology for the expansion. In 1969, the final decision to use PWRs under a Westinghouse licence was reached. Later on, the reactors were adapted and “franced” — by the 1980s, production had achieved a reasonable degree of local autonomy.Flamanville nuclear power station under construction, August 1980. Photo: Jacques Lemière / Archives départementales de la Manche, fonds 115 Fi. Source.The build-out itself was carried out in the same manner as all the other post-war transformations: centralised, strategic, massive. EDF (Électricité de France) was basically the state-owned national utility. To fund its enormous effort, it was authorised to borrow enormous sums. The amount of borrowed capital was so huge that by 1976, EDF was the third-biggest borrower on the US capital market — right after Ford and General Motors.Make no mistake — France did not predict the oil crisis, nor did it slide through it. At the time, the energy price spikes did really bite. Yet in March of 1974, when then-prime minister Pierre Messmer announced an acceleration of the build-out, there was infrastructure in place to be accelerated.The build-up wasn’t flawless: the speed and the directive manner backfired, sparking various protests across the country. One major flashpoint was Superphénix — a new form of reactor that ran on the principle of “fast” neutrons and used a much newer and more experimental technology. Yet it wasn’t the only thing people were mad about.It was the non-consensual policy that made people angry: both intellectuals and the working class from rural areas. Specifically, this happened at Plogoff, near Pointe du Raz, where EDF was planning a four-reactor nuclear power station. The locals viewed this as a risk of land expropriation and disruption to fishing. Soon enough, the protests spun out of control, and after years of tension, the project was called off in 1981.Anti-nuclear campaign posters from Plogoff: boycott, confrontation and solidarity. Source: SKREO-Dz. The first two also appear in Plogoff’s municipal archive; the third is credited to Pierrick Le Corre by Musée départemental breton.Nuclear power was probably France’s most successful 1970s bet. Energy security drove the programme; lower-carbon electricity became another lasting benefit. Yet it became a backbone of the country’s autonomy and reduced volatility & external dependence, setting France apart from its neighbours.French electricity production, 1980–2023. Chart: Theanphibian / Wikimedia Commons, public domain. Data: U.S. Energy Information Administration.To this day, French power plants are monuments to Cold War-era futurism that actually became part of the economy and didn’t disappear. And surprisingly, some of them look really nice for the industrial monstrosities those things are always considered to be. It could be the beautiful landscape around them that is doing the job, or the more elegant architecture the French are famous for. But probably both.Paluel nuclear power station, Normandy, 2005. Photo: Francis Chanteloup (EDF) / Energi-vore, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.Cruas-Meysse nuclear power station, 2012. Photo: Yelkrokoyade / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.Minitel: online before the webI’m trying to get a table at Le Ventre de l’Architecte at the famous Le Corbusier house. The opening hours are wild: 12–2 pm, 7:30–9:15 pm, meaning you’d better get hungry when the place is open. After reading a bunch of unhinged comments from the restaurant manager (check their reviews on Google, it’s just fire), I navigate to the website. As a person who led a premium web studio, I am disappointed but not surprised by what I see. A question that pops up in my mind: was the French internet any good?Spoiler: hell yes.When we think about the early days of the internet and picture its mass adoption, we immediately imagine the US. Yet France brought online services into millions of homes well before the web became an everyday habit.Minitel was a European predecessor of the World Wide Web. It kicked off at the beginning of the 1980s. As a telephone subscriber, you could get one of the Minitel terminals for free. This wouldn’t be a regular PC: no apps or games on the device, just a b&w text interface for online services. Its design had practical limits: screen designer Jean-Yves Michalik described the 40-column display and an alphabetic keyboard that was later replaced with AZERTY.Thomson terminal used in the Télétel trial, Vélizy, 22 November 1980. Photo: Bernard Marti, CC BY 3.0.Minitel terminals were originally a fancy replacement for the paper directory. People would get hooked on additional functions like purchasing train tickets or making bookings pretty randomly, after their usual phone number searches. Apparently, this was a great strategy for adoption: by 1989, France had around five million Minitel terminals. By 1993, that figure had grown to almost 6.5 million, with terminals in 20% of households.https://medium.com/media/32699826694b1587b4b4312597f62cc3/hrefMinitel was no random accident. It was part of a visionary digital transformation, imagined, described and delivered by the French state in order to bring a futuristic reality into everyday life. “The Computerisation of Society”, a report that came out in 1978, explored the emergence of an information society. The report contained a blueprint of how the mass adoption of computers would shift many gears in societal interaction, how business would change and how politics would follow. It also considered the infrastructure and political choices that this transformation would require.That report captured the ambition behind France’s push into networked computing.One of the things Minitel would give birth to was anonymous dating chats. Or, as they called them, “pink chats”. Users would assume they were speaking with someone who was who they said they were, which was not always the case.Minitel’s early success did not turn into global dominance. Its dedicated terminals and centrally organised network made online services accessible, but eventually faced competition from personal computers and the open web. An OECD assessment pointed to ageing technology, high usage charges and limited export markets. The system that had made getting online simple also had limits.The last official year of Minitel was 2012. That was a surprisingly long life for a network born at the beginning of the 1980s.Nowadays: winds of European tech sovereigntyOne thing that caught my eye in Marseille was how many things are called “Mistral”, from navy ships you can see docked in the harbour to local soda brands and driving schools that have this word in their name.It’s a special, even holy word for many francophones. Mistral is the name of a strong, cold & mighty Mediterranean wind that blows all across Provence.Also, Mistral is the name of one of the few European frontier AI labs. As I write this text, the fourth generation of its Large model has been announced, adding another chapter to France’s ambitions in computing.Mistral AI Now Summit, Paris, 28 May 2026. Source: Mistral AIIt’s too early to predict whether the new European bet on open-weight sovereign models and an application layer for robotics and manufacturing will win the future.But at least we know that writing the future was once in fashion in Europe.Why not again?Further readingBritish Airways: Celebrating Concorde — the aircraft and its service history.Andrée Putman: Le Concorde Air France — the cabin redesign.IAEA: France country profile — the nuclear programme and reactor choices.Archives départementales du Finistère: Plogoff — the proposed plant and opposition.OECD: Minitel assessment — adoption, economics and limitations.Jean-Yves Michalik: Minitel screen design — a contemporary practitioner’s account.Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise
item.description: A product team weighs a purchased tool against an internal build at the same table.Artificial intelligence made building cheap and buying easy. The trade-off now turns on who owns the upkeep, the seams between tools, the chat surfaces, and the data.For most of my career, product management owned buy versus build. A product manager wrote the case, finance checked the math, and procurement signed.Designers arrived after the decision was made, inherited whatever won, and spent years sanding its rough edges. Artificial intelligence changed the math on both sides at once.Build is cheaper now, but the yearly upkeep never shows up in the business case.Buy comes with legacy, and that legacy now includes someone else’s model, roadmap, and release calendar. And usually there’s a third option nobody names: replacing the system you already have.2025: The State of Generative AI in the EnterpriseMenlo Ventures found in 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise that 76% of enterprise artificial intelligence use cases were purchased rather than built, up from 53% a year earlier. Meanwhile, coding agents make a working internal tool look like an afternoon project.More work happens inside Teams, Slack, Claude, and ChatGPT, surfaces neither option owns.Don’t ask which option costs less, Ask where the complexity lands: in your code, in a vendor’s roadmap, or on your users.Budget for Build MaintenanceA designer with a coding agent can now stand up an internal tool before a vendor’s sales team returns the call. Andrej Karpathy named that loose style vibe coding in 2025, and Simon Willison drew the line in Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (but vibe coding rocks). Prototypes can be loose, but code you keep has to be read like any other.Most internal tools become code you keep, which makes them products. It needs a budget, an owner, and someone to call when it breaks. Most teams don’t think of it that way, because nobody bought anything.I learned this the hard way.We built an internal workflow application in one place I worked at, before AI, because nothing we could buy matched how our teams worked. It shipped fast, people came to depend on it, and that’s exactly when it became a nightmare to maintain.Every new approval step meant changing code few people understood, small fixes broke things elsewhere, and nobody had budgeted time for any of it.That’s where my rule comes from. I budget 30% of the upfront build cost every year for upkeep: updates, patches, model changes, and new requests.The math isn’t as straightword as it seems.Run that math and many vibe-coded apps cost more than the subscriptions they replace. Say two people spend two weeks at a fully loaded $150 an hour, which is $24,000 up front and $7,200 a year after. A subscription at $20 a seat for 25 people runs $6,000 a year. Over three years, the build costs $45,600 against $18,000, and only one of them came with a support team.Every generated line is a line somebody has to own, and the initial owner usually doesn’t want that responsibility.Open source taught this lesson first. Black Duck’s 2026 Open Source Security and Risk Analysis Report found open source in 98% of audited codebases, and 93% held components with no development activity in two years.In 2024, a backdoor reached the widely used XZ Utils library after an attacker spent years earning its maintainer’s trust. Generated code has the same weakness: nobody paid for it, so nobody budgeted to watch it. Google’s 2025 DORA Report found adoption of artificial intelligence still hurts delivery stability.Accept the Vendor’s LegacyBuying looks like the cautious choice, and often it is.Purchases from specialized vendors succeeded about 67% of the time, while internal builds succeeded about a third as often, according to research from MIT’s NANDA initiative covered in Fortune’s MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing.The fair objection is selection, since companies tend to buy for well-understood problems and build for messy ones, which flatters vendors. Hold the number loosely, but the direction matches where enterprise budgets went.A purchase is never only a feature set. You also get the vendor’s data model, release cadence, and theory of what your users are trying to do.When you buy, you import another company’s organization chart.Systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them, as Melvin Conway observed in 1968. Your users end up inside a product tuned for that company’s largest customers, who may look nothing like yours.Measure the Tool GapsUsers don’t experience your build or your purchase on its own. They experience the gaps. You can count those gaps the way you’d count clicks in a usability test: pick one real task, follow it across systems, and log every switch and every retyped value.How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications?The gaps add up fast.People in a 2022 study of 137 workers on 20 teams at three Fortune 500 companies switched between applications and websites roughly 1,200 times a day. Reorienting after each switch cost them just under four hours a week, about 9% of their working time, according to How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications? in Harvard Business Review and AAPL Leadership.Homegrown tools widen the gaps too. In the 1990s, departments built their own Microsoft Access databases because waiting on the central technology team took a quarter.The databases worked until their authors changed jobs, and then the data inside them became one more place nobody could reach. Today’s version is drift: patterns that stop matching the rest of the product and error states nobody designed.Complexity always lands somewhere, and the only choice is where.Complexity is conserved, and the only real choice is who absorbs it. That’s Larry Tesler’s law.A build moves complexity into your codebase, while a purchase moves it into someone else’s roadmap. A careless mix of both moves it onto your users, one copy-and-paste at a time. Before anyone argues about license fees, ask where the complexity ends up under each option.Design for Host SurfacesIn many organizations, the place people meet your product is no longer your product. It’s Teams, Slack, Claude, or ChatGPT.Apps moved inside ChatGPT conversations in 2025 with OpenAI’s Introducing apps in ChatGPT and the new Apps SDK. In January 2026, MCP Apps — Bringing UI Capabilities To MCP Clients let tools return interactive interfaces that render inside Claude and ChatGPT. Build or buy, your most-used screen may end up as a card in someone else’s window.I’ve worked inside this arrangement before. I designed the developer documentation site for Myspace, whose 2008 developer platform let third-party applications run on member profiles. The host set the box size, the permissions, and what an app could know about the person looking at it. Every app was designed inside that frame, and chat surfaces are drawing it again.The host draws the frame, and your job is deciding what fits inside it.The rules are specific, and they belong to the host. An inline card in ChatGPT gets at most two actions, no nested scrolling, the system font, and a logo the host adds for you, per OpenAI’s UI guidelines for the Apps SDK.A Slack message holds up to 50 blocks under Block Kit. Microsoft’s Types of Cards & their Usage names Adaptive Cards the recommended card type for new Teams development.People expect your product to work like the places where they spend most of their time, which is Jakob Nielsen’s Jakob’s Law of Internet User Experience. Inside a chat surface, that stops being advice, because the host’s patterns are the only ones on offer. So design the card as its own product, with one job, one primary action, and a handoff to your full application when the task outgrows it.Count the Replacement CostMost of these decisions aren’t made on empty ground. Something already exists, and the real question is whether to replace it. Replacement carries costs that appear in neither column.The first cost is lost expertise. Task time falls with repetition, which is the Power Law of Practice covered on my UX Guidelines site (@usabilitycounts), and your power users have years of repetitions in the old tool. Replace it, and they start the curve over, usually in the busiest quarter.The second cost is hidden rules. You shouldn’t tear down a fence until you know why it went up, as G. K. Chesterton argued in 1929. Old enterprise software is full of fences, and each one was a rule somebody once needed.The new thing always wins the demo against the tool people already know.The third cost is our own bias. People value their amateur work about as highly as experts’ work, according to Michael Norton and his co-authors in The IKEA Effect: When Labor Leads to Love. Melissa Perri described the organizational version in The Build Trap: building is the easy part, and teams get rewarded for shipping instead of for learning what customers need.Not invented here makes it worse. Not invented here is the reflex of rejecting an outside solution because someone else made it. Ralph Katz and Thomas Allen tracked 50 research and development project groups for An empirical test of the Not Invented Here (NIH) Syndrome, a 1980 MIT working paper.Groups that had worked together five or more years performed significantly worse, and they talked less with professionals outside the team. Coding agents lower the price of acting on that reflex, because rebuilding a vendor’s feature now takes a weekend instead of a budget cycle.Coding agents also distort the estimate. Who knew?Coding agents also distort the estimate. Experienced developers took 19% longer on real tasks with the tools, yet estimated afterward they had been 20% faster, in METR’s randomized trial Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity.It’s one study of 16 developers, and METR now flags it as out of date. Still, price your own prototype the way you’d price a stranger’s.Buy Commodities, Build DifferentiatorsThe clearest test I know comes from Simon Wardley (@swardley). In Finding a path, he sorts components from genesis to custom built to product to commodity.His shorthand for building commodities yourself is Thomas Thwaites, the designer who spent nine months trying to build a toaster from raw materials. A coding agent shrinks the nine months to a weekend, which matters less than it seems, because you still own every repair after it ships.Coding agents change the toaster math, not the toaster.For products built on artificial intelligence, the map has a clear split. The model is sliding toward commodity, rented by the token. The experience around it is still custom: how a suggestion explains itself, how someone corrects it, and whether people trust it. A competitor can’t copy that by signing the same contract.Building still wins in a few places. Build when your own data is the advantage and a vendor would have to hold it to use it.Build when regulation rules out every product on the market, and build the moments you compete on. If a feature would look the same in every competitor’s product, though, it’s probably a commodity.Those cases also assume you have the people, and most organizations don’t. Vibe coding gets you a demo, not the skills a production artificial intelligence application needs: retrieval over messy records, evaluations, permissions, and monitoring.Source: IBM Global AI Adoption Index 2023IBM surveyed 8,584 technology professionals for Data Suggests Growth in Enterprise Adoption of AI is Due to Widespread Deployment by Early Adopters, published in January 2024. Limited skills and expertise topped the barriers at 33%, with data complexity next at 25%. The more data an application touches, the wider that gap gets.Map Where Data LivesA model can only answer from what it can see, so the experience follows wherever your data lives. Buy a tool and your records sit in the vendor’s schema, reachable on the vendor’s terms.Build one and the data stays yours, along with the job of governing it. When Anthropic announced the Model Context Protocol in 2024, it described models cut off from data trapped behind silos and legacy systems.So run the landing test a second time, aimed at the data. A card in Teams is only as useful as the permissions behind it, and an assistant that can’t reach the contract can’t summarize it.Whoever holds the records decides what any surface can show.Regulation is starting to price this in. The law has applied since September 12, 2025, and switching charges between data processing providers, including data egress fees, end entirely on January 12, 2027, according to the European Commission’s Data Act explained.Leaving a vendor is getting cheaper on paper. In practice, a migration is mostly a data project with a UX bill attached: renamed fields, lost history, and reports that no longer match.Before any contract, ask where the data will live, who can export it and in what format, and whether the surfaces your people already use can reach it.Those answers shape the experience more than the feature list does.Prepare for Model RetirementEither way, part of your product now runs on something you don’t control. Build on a model and that model will be retired. Anthropic promises at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a publicly released model.Four Years of Frontier Model Releases to Maintain. This slide makes me dizzy. How do you maintain this?Its Model deprecations page lists the Claude Sonnet 4.5 snapshot from September 2025 as deprecated on September 30, 2026, with retirement set for November 30, 2026.Buy a product built on a model and the same thing happens, one layer removed and on the vendor’s schedule. Tone shifts. Refusals move. Summaries grow or shrink, and edge cases that used to pass start failing. A vendor’s release notes may not mention a model change at all, so ask in the contract how much notice you’ll get.A model swap is a redesign nobody scheduled, and now happens on a frequent basis. Maintenane is now a real time activity.The exit plan belongs to design, not only to procurement. Keep a set of real user tasks with known good outcomes, run them against every new model or vendor release, and review the results the way you’d review a usability study. Twenty or thirty tasks is enough to start, as long as they include the common requests, the expensive mistakes, and the cases where the correct response is to decline.Decide Where Complexity LandsBuy versus build used to end at the signature or at launch. Now neither choice finishes, because the parts keep moving after the decision. Building got cheaper and stayed expensive to own. Buying got easier and arrived carrying more of someone else’s history than the demo let on.So the decision can’t stay with product management and finance. The numbers in that spreadsheet are real enough. They just leave out the costs users feel most: drift in tools nobody maintains, expertise lost when an old system goes away, data stuck where new tools can’t reach it, and chat surfaces whose layout rules you don’t set.Designers, product managers, and researchers are the people who see those costs first. They can also measure them, in task time and in the moments where someone gives up. Bring that evidence to the decision before it’s made, not after it ships.The landing test won’t tell you whether to buy or build. It tells you where the complexity will go, so somebody can be standing there on purpose. Most of the time, that points toward buying the commodity and building the difference. The seams between the two are yours either way, so design them.Action ItemsTest vendors against prototypes. Run a hands-on bake-off with real tasks, using the scenario-based method in The Right Way to Select Technology by Tony Byrne and Jarrod Gingras. Enter your current system and a quick internal prototype alongside the vendors, and ask the current system’s heaviest users why each odd step exists.List every system touched. Pick one real task and follow it from start to finish. Write down each system it passes through, where each value is stored, and who can export it, then put that list in the business case next to the license fee.Budget 30% for upkeep. Before a build ships, name the person who maintains it and set aside 30% of its build cost every year. Treat that line as fixed, the way you would a subscription, so fixes and library updates don’t wait for spare time.Retest after model changes. Keep 20 to 30 real tasks with known good answers, including the common requests and the costly mistakes. Run them whenever a model or vendor release changes what’s underneath, and review the results like a usability study.Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: A founder with a tool is not a founder with a clue
item.description: Somewhere in this room is the one person who can tell if any of it is actually good. AI made everyone else look exactly like them.AI lets a solo founder produce a product, but it can’t help them understand whether that product is actually good…yet. That expertise, the hard-won judgment underneath it, has always been what decides who wins and who quietly (or epically) fails.There’s a movement in the startup world that currently claims if you can’t build your product by yourself, with AI, you shouldn’t be building it at all. The “advice” suggests that a solo founder should handle coding, design, and marketing with AI and should not hire a traditional team at all.Hiring someone to design or engineer your product, whether it’s an agency, a contractor, or an early employee, is treated as proof you don’t really understand your own product and a growing number of investors won’t back a founder who would do that.Most founders are doing exactly what they’ve been told works, and often they don’t know any better. The idea that needing help is a weakness sets a tone that will eventually backfire because most people are not unicorns, because unicorns do not exist.Paul Graham, who founded Y Combinator, has said for years that he prefers founders who can build the thing themselves. Carles Reina, an early backer of ElevenLabs, told CNBC his first instant red flag is a founder who “literally cannot build products.” More than a third of new startups are now solo-founded, because AI made it possible to go from idea to working product without the people who used to be required.Buried in that whole position is an assumption that’s dangerously misguided. It assumes that because you can now produce the thing, you have the expertise to know whether the thing is any good. Those have never been the same thing.AI collapsed the cost of making something to almost nothing, but it did nothing to impact the cost of judgment, the years of studying how people behave, what makes a product feel trustworthy.We got product creation for free, but forgot that expertise didn’t come with it.Being able to vibe-code an app over a weekend makes you an expert in exactly one thing. Can you guess? It’s in vibe-coding an app over a weekend.I lean on these tools as hard as anyone, on fast, super AI-heavy schedules that pressure test the technology every day. Even at that speed, it’s obvious how often what comes out is close but not right, and how often it takes real experience and hard-won knowledge to catch the difference and make the call.None of this is a knock on the founders who build a product themselves. Seriously, kudos to them. A founder who vibe-codes their idea into something real is doing something genuinely good, they’re getting what’s in their head out into the world, fast, and that has always been the hard part.The trouble starts when the people funding them treat that first draft as the finished product, and think asking for help is a weakness.AI moves the thinking rather than removing it. The people cheering the death of the expert have confused two different things, making what you asked for, and knowing whether what got made is any good.They’re not wrong about the easy part. One person really can produce what used to take a crowd.Where they’re rightDario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has said he thinks the first billion-dollar company run by a single person could arrive as soon as 2026, and he put the odds at something like seventy to eighty percent. He has an obvious stake in that being true and his company creates tools that would make it possible, but nevertheless, the prediction could be realistic.Venture capitalist and Harvard Business School professor, Jeff Bussgang, has described the same shift from the investing side, right down to a betting pool among his tech-CEO friends over the year the first one-person billion-dollar company shows up.The cost of producing software, a brand, a marketing campaign, a working prototype, has fallen through the floor. A founder with the right AI stack can now do in a weekend what used to take a team a quarter.Andreessen Horowitz says that building has gotten so cheap that founders now skip the questions they used to have to answer first. Their Speedrun team’s perspective is that the interesting question is no longer “can you build it,” because the answer is now always yes. The interesting, and perhaps more important question is “should you,” which is what it’s always been. Marty Cagan has been telling product teams for decades that the job is to ask not just whether you can build the thing, but whether you should build it at all.When making the thing is nearly free, the discipline shifts from execution to judgment about what deserves to exist at all.The money has unsurprisingly moved accordingly. At TechCrunch Disrupt, seed investors including Elizabeth Yin urged early-stage founders to lean on AI coding leverage as much as they can, and Renata Quintini of Renegade Partners agreed it’s the right move for finding product-market fit, rather than spending early cash on headcount they don’t yet need.Rebecca Lynn points out that it’s never been easier to stand up a company “in demo mode,” which is exactly why she’s careful about what she funds.The thing these investors are reacting to is that a lot of the roles that used to be mandatory at the start of a company are now optional, or at least deferrable.Startups have a long history of getting too big, too early. The Startup Genome Report, which analyzed more than 3,200 startups, found that premature scaling, hiring too many people too soon is the single most common reason startups fail.Starting with a small team is generally smarter, but a founder who can build the first version themselves, who understands the problem because they live it, who doesn’t need to hire a translator to turn their idea into a thing, has a real and durable advantage.The clearest case is the technical founder building for people exactly like themselves, the engineer making tools for engineers, who is both the builder and the user and genuinely doesn’t need anyone in between.The trend is shifting to the founder building it alone, but the reality is they often shouldn’t.Travis Howell and Todd Hall looked at whether solo founders can hold their own against co-founded teams, and found that they can, under one condition, when the solo founder has deep, broad experience to draw on.It works when the founder’s real expertise is in building the thing, the craft, the risks, the details that make a product good, not just in the problem it solves. A technical founder building for engineers can do it, because what they know maps onto what the product needs.Knowing an industry cold, or a market, or a customer, is valuable, but it is not the same as knowing how to build something people want to use.Right now, the industry keeps confusing the two. Thinking a tool will fix it is just foolish.Telling a founder that reaching out for help, from someone who could genuinely add qualified perspective or experience, is a red flag gets it backwards. It punishes a person for not personally holding every bit of knowledge a company needs, which is a bar no real human should be held to.Forty people felt busier. Eight people shipped it.Eight people in a conference roomOn a Saturday morning in 1999, five of us met at iXL’s offices in Manhattan’s Union Square to stage a quiet coup. We picked the day on purpose. The place was empty, no account directors, really nobody around to hear what we were about to do. Just us gathered around a table voluntarily sequestered in a conference room to discuss a project we thought we could save by making it smaller.iXL was one of those agencies that got enormous by swallowing other agencies, which is what was common during dot-com 1.0. Agency size wasn’t a virtue or a sin, it was just the reality of the industry. The project we were on had at least forty people attached to it, with one of the largest budgets in the company, and it was sinking under its own weight.There was too much process, too many people who had to be looped in before decisions could be made, a launch date that kept on sliding.This wasn’t a new phenomenon (not that I knew that at the time). In 1975, computer scientist Fred Brooks watched IBM try to rescue a late software project by adding programmers, and watched it get later. He turned it into Brooks’s Law, which says that adding people late to a project just makes it even later.It’s a brutal, mathematical reality. As you add people, each new person you add has to be brought up to speed, which pulls the people who already know what they’re doing away from the work. Every new person adds a communication line to every other person, so the coordination cost climbs faster than the output does.Forty people don’t move four times faster than ten. They move slower, they cause blockers left and right, but they feel busier doing it.We wanted to cut the team to eight, with severe focus. Eight specialists, each the best in the building at one specific thing. The cast list we wanted:A front-end developerA couple of back-end developersA project managerAn information architect (which is what you called a UX designer back then)An art directorA creative directorA designerThe premise wasn’t to fire the other forty members of the team. They’d have plenty of work to do on what was next on the roadmap, but to actually ship this thing, we needed the smallest possible group of people who each could use their expertise to collaborate and move this forward smarter and faster.Years later, Amazon would make this famous as the two-pizza team, Jeff Bezos’s rule that no team should be bigger than two pizzas can feed, somewhere around ten people, because that’s the size that stays fast.I was twenty-three. I was nowhere near the most senior person in that room, though I was somehow the most senior information architect on the project in all of New York, which should tell you how little a title and actual expertise have to do with each other.I was also, for the record, a bit of a troublemaker, which is how you end up in an empty office on a Saturday trying to shrink your own project by eighty percent. We wrote the plan, we walked our account director through it, and somehow he said yes.Then we had to go do it, and we did.That little team became a precision instrument the company reached for whenever something hard had to get built fast, and I’m confident it made them a lot of money.As for the giants that were busy getting bigger, most of them did not make it. iXL shrank drastically. MarchFirst, the largest of these roll-ups, a nine-thousand-person, six-billion-dollar web consultancy, burned through a billion and a half dollars in fourteen months and filed the biggest bankruptcy in the industry’s history.The whole sector contracted by seventy to eighty percent. Being huge turned out to be the most expensive way to be fragile.That is all to say, the idea of small, nimble teams is rarely a bad idea, so when a venture capitalist says a founder doesn’t need forty people, I can’t argue with that.The thing to understand is the strategy of what we did in that room, because that is not the argument for the solo founder show being encouraged today.We cut forty people down to eight experts. The pitch today is to cut it down to one founder and a tool. Those may sound similar, but one of them concentrates expertise, while the other removes it and hopes the software quietly fills the hole where it used to be.Patrick Neeman argues that in the age of AI, when anyone can stand up the same model and the same features, the thing that sets your product apart is the experience and the judgment built around it. You own what differentiates you, the workflows, the design, the taste, the deep understanding of your user, and you buy or borrow the commodity underneath.The mistake in the solo-founder pitch is assuming the tool handed you the part that differentiates. All it really handed you was a commodity.Ethan Mollick, who is about as bullish on AI at work as anyone, insists that AI rewards expertise. It lets the people who already know what good looks like judge the output, catch the confident mistakes, and push the tool past its defaults, while everyone else takes whatever the machine hands them.The AI builds you a slick dashboard and never thinks to ask what it looks like before there’s any data in it, or when something breaks. It gives you a clean screen with light gray text on white, and someone who knows catches that a lot of your users can’t read it. That stuff only gets caught when someone with real experience is deciding whether it’s actually done or even takes the time to ask the AI to review it.Tao An, a researcher at Hawaii Pacific University, lays out the split cleanly, saying that on routine work, AI lifts a beginner up to a competent floor, which is real and useful. On the hard, judgment-heavy work, however, the kind that decides whether a product is actually good, it does the opposite. It widens the gap between the person who knows what they’re doing and the person who doesn’t, because only one of them can tell when the confident-looking answer is wrong.The tool amplifies the expertise in the room. It does not supply it.At the end of the day, this comes down to one thing: the expertise has to be in the room. An employee, a contractor, a cofounder, a partner, or you, if you genuinely have it. Assemble it however you want, and keep the team as small as the work allows. The tool will make almost anything you ask it to. What it cannot do is tell you whether the thing is any good. That part has always belonged to the people who know, and it still does.Paul Rand gave Steve Jobs one logo and the reasoning behind it, not a menu. This is the menu.The thing you can’t promptIn 1986, Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT, the company he started after being pushed out of Apple. He hired Paul Rand, probably the most famous graphic designer alive, and asked him for a few options to choose from. Rand said no. He would solve the problem, he told Jobs, hand back a single answer and Jobs could take it or leave it.He charged a hundred thousand dollars. He came back with one design, a black cube tilted at twenty-eight degrees, presented in a bound book that walked Jobs through every decision, why the word, why the lowercase “e,” why the angle, until the logo felt less like a choice and more like the only possible conclusion.Jobs, who genuinely had plenty of taste himself, paid six figures for something he couldn’t produce on his own. Whatever was in his head, he could have generated a thousand tilted cubes before lunch, but the reasoning underneath that piece of design derived from years of accumulated judgment that let Rand know, with total confidence, which single answer was right and why.This is the gap the whole “just build it yourself” argument ignores. Producing the deliverable (whatever it may be) and knowing whether the deliverable is good are completely different skills.Right now, you can easily generate a logo, a landing page, an entire app, in an afternoon. What you cannot necessarily do is hold the judgment to look at what came out and know that the hierarchy is off, that the flow asks too much of a tired person, that the tone is wrong for the people you’re trying to reach, that the confident, finished-looking thing on your screen is quietly, expensively broken or costing you customers.Christian Holst found that the average checkout asks for around eleven form fields when most need eight, and that nearly one in five people abandon a purchase simply because the process felt too long. In testing, cutting a form from eleven fields to four lifted completions by 120 percent. The tool that built you that form has no idea it’s costing you customers.AI makes everything it spits out look “good.” It can be clean, modern, professional, but that’s not always a perk. It’s also pulling from the same places everyone else is pulling from. When everyone builds with the same tools, trained on the same examples, everything starts to look the same.Aurelie Radom suggests that AI may not have democratized design judgment, but it did democratize output, and when the models are all trained on the same stuff, the output space compresses and products that have nothing to do with each other start converging on the same shapes and the same layouts.Alwin de Rooij and Michael Mose Biskjaer compared nineteen studies around this and found the effect is real and very measurable. The more people lean on the same AI, the more their work converges, which means looking finished and modern is fast becoming the least distinctive thing a product can be.Looking finished used to mean something, odds were decent that someone who knew what they were doing added a contextual lens. That’s not true anymore. AI gives you the finished look in seconds, whether or not a single smart decision went into it.Humans, it turns out, are built to fall for this distraction. In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura put a set of interface layouts in front of people and found the better-looking ones got rated as easier to use, even when they flat-out weren’t. They called it the aesthetic-usability effect.We see something attractive and our brain quietly decides it works.AI produces attractive by default, which means it produces trust it hasn’t earned because the thing it created looks great, you believe it’s good, but there’s no proof it actually will work.Fabrizio Dell’Acqua, Ethan Mollick, and their colleagues studied 758 consultants and found that on the tasks AI is bad at, the ones who relied on it did worse than the ones who didn’t. The AI gave them wrong answers that looked right, and the people who couldn’t tell the difference used them anyway.Separately, Yue Liu and colleagues studied a large batch of AI-written code and found it full of quality and maintainability problems hiding under a finished surface.This isn’t a secret in our field. Nicole Alexandra Michaelis calls it the “taste paradox,” where we all agree that knowing what’s good is the skill that matters most now, and we’ve built a way of working that keeps people from ever learning it. The more you lean on AI to tell you what works, the less you ever figure out how to tell on your own.Ruiqi Zhou adds a business lens to this, saying that if everyone can make the same thing, making it isn’t an advantage anymore. The only thing still worth anything is the judgment to know what’s worth making.After AI, everyone could launch. The products that were actually good still came from teams.The receiptsThis isn’t an emotional argument about how things look. The numbers back it up. The business value of expertise is one of the most heavily documented things in product, and the data got sharper once AI showed up.Hyunso Kim, Hyo Kang, and Jaeyong Song studied more than 160,000 product launches on Product Hunt, before and after ChatGPT arrived, and found that after AI showed up, solo launches spiked, especially in categories that used to require a team, but when they looked at quality, at which products actually reached the top tier, teams still dominated, as much as ever.AI widened the door for solo entry and did nothing to close the quality gap. More things got made. The good things still came from the people with the expertise to make them good.The money follows the same pattern. First Round Capital studied a decade of its own portfolio and found that companies with more than one founder outperformed solo founders by 163 percent, raised more, and grew faster, an advantage they tie directly to complementary skill and the sharper decisions it produces. Their data says the opposite of their advice.That’s not a nostalgia story about the pre-AI days. Boston Consulting Group found that the companies leading in AI, the ones it calls “future-built,” are outgrowing their competitors by 1.7 times in revenue and 3.6 times in shareholder return.These winners used real expertise to aim the new tools and didn’t just buy the tools to replace the expertise.Benedict Sheppard, Hugo Sarrazin, Garen Kouyoumjian, and Fabricio Dore scored hundreds of companies on how seriously they treat design, then tracked their results over five years. The ones that took design most seriously grew revenue about a third faster than the ones that didn’t, and returned more than half again as much to their shareholders.The same research shows why those winners are so rare. More than forty percent of companies still don’t talk to their users while they’re building, and over half have no real way to tell whether their own team’s work is any good.Taking design seriously is what separates the winners from everyone else. Taking design seriously means being able to judge whether your design is actually working. Most companies can’t or just don’t.If most companies can’t tell good design from bad in the first place, then of course they’ll believe AI made them something good. They have no way to know it didn’t.Judgment is not the same as one powerful person’s gut, and the answer to “the tool can’t decide for you” is not “so let the loudest opinion in the room decide instead.” In 2009, Google’s lead designer Doug Bowman quit and explained why in a post called “Goodbye, Google.” The company, he wrote, couldn’t choose between two shades of blue, so it tested forty-one.He’d been asked to prove, with data, whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide. That’s the opposite mistake, and it’s just as bad. When no one on the team can just say “four,” you test everything, because nobody has the expertise, trust or standing to make the call.Real expertise is knowing which decisions you can settle and move on from in a second and which ones actually need testing.Here’s the one who can tell. There are only ever a few of them, and no tool has replaced one yet.Build small. Just bring the expertise.Rick Rubin has produced some of the most important records of the last forty years, across rock, rap, country, and pop, with artists such as Johnny Cash, Jay-Z, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Adele.When Anderson Cooper asked him, on 60 Minutes, whether he could play instruments or work a soundboard, Rubin said no. “I have no technical ability,” he said. “And I know nothing about music.”Cooper, reasonably, asked what he was being paid for. Rubin’s answer sums up why an expert lens matters. He said, “The confidence that I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.”He can’t compose the tracks himself, but he is one of the most sought-after people in music anyway, because composition isn’t always the point. Judgment is.The ability to sit with a thing and know, with conviction, what it needs and what’s getting in the way is the rarest and most valuable thing in any creative endeavor. It is exactly the thing that does not reside in a tool, no matter how good the tool gets.The people telling founders they don’t need anyone but themselves and AI are half right in a way that matters. You certainly don’t need forty people. You may not even need ten. It’s fair to say that the bloat they’re concerned about is real, and killing that is good, but they’ve taken a true thing about team size and turned it into a false thing about expertise.Fewer people, yes. Less expertise, no.Right now, AI gives you the output of expertise without the expertise. It hands you the artifact a skilled person would have made, without the judgment that skilled person would use to know whether the artifact is any good.That gap is real today, and it is real for the foreseeable future, though I won’t pretend to know how long “foreseeable” lasts. Maybe the models close it, maybe judgment turns out to be the last thing to automate.Either way, you have to build in the world you’re actually in, and in this one, AI can make the thing, but it cannot tell you if the thing is good.Founders actually doing this are the first to admit where it breaks. Anik Devaughn, who built an AI-native commerce platform largely by himself, said that founders who understand their business deeply can move faster and stay smaller, but the ones who can’t evaluate the work will just automate bad decisions.Basically, if you’re a founder talking to an investor who says they won’t back anyone who hires help, the investor is missing the point.A founder who can tell the difference between what’s working and what isn’t is a far safer bet than one who can only tell you the demo they put together looks great.This is not an argument for hiring an agency, or hiring anyone in particular. It’s an argument for embracing the expertise that has to be there to create success. It can be an employee or a contractor, a cofounder or a partner, or you, if you’ve genuinely put in the years.NYU Professor J.P. Eggers ran an experiment where MBA students used AI agents to build startups from scratch. The AI was good at discrete tasks and fast brainstorming, he found, but it couldn’t replace the judgment that comes from having real specialists in the room.His line for what happens without them sums up a lot, saying “You’re kind of taking it on faith that what the AI is producing is pretty good.”Assemble the smallest team you can. Keep it lean enough to move fast, and make sure someone on it can tell what’s right from what’s broken. AI can build anything. Knowing if it’s right takes a human.AI or not, it all falls apart without someone who actually knows what they’re doing.Anyone who treats a founder’s willingness to bring in that person as weakness has it backwards. A founder who knows what they don’t know, and goes and gets the help, is the one worth betting on.References and further readingThe belief that you should build it yourselfDiana Bocco, AI Is Letting Solo Founders Build Startups Without Hiring (Inc.).
